description: Passionate about software development, full-stack development, AI, and building creative, interactive applications that solve real-world problems. Experienced with React, JavaScript, Python, Firebase, database management, and computer vision.
summary: Marswalk is a surface-excursion planner for the first astronauts on Mars. NASA has decades of Mars data, but today’s tools, such as Mars Trek, are built for regional and global views, not the few hundred metres an astronaut covers on one walk. Marswalk plans one walk at the delta front of Jezero Crater, where Perseverance is exploring an ancient river delta. It layers six kinds of NASA data on one screen, turns NASA’s elevation model into a slope hazard map, and plans a route around steep ground: only 73 m of our route is on slopes over 10°, against 310 m for straight lines between the stops. Astronauts can preview the walk in 3D, get a go/no-go decision from daylight, dust, radiation and suit time, see real rover photos of each stop, and log samples and field notes. Safety comes first for NASA, and a walk planned on the right data is both safer and better for science.
details:
What it does. Marswalk plans a round-trip walk from a habitat to three science stops at Jezero Crater: 1.50 km, 42 m of climb, 13° at its steepest, about 2 h 26 min including science time. Astronauts can add stops anywhere in the surveyed zone and the route re-plans.

How it works.

  • A Python script reads NASA’s 20 m elevation model of Jezero and calculates the slope of every patch of ground: green under 10°, amber 10–20°, red over 20°.
  • An A* path search, run in the browser, finds the easiest route between stops. Walking time slows on slopes using Tobler’s hiking function.
  • The map layers HiRISE (25 cm) and CTX (6 m) imagery, THEMIS day and night infrared, and the slope hazard. Each layer can be switched and faded.
  • An elevation profile shows the climb along the route; the scale bar is calibrated for Mars.
  • A 3D view shapes the elevation data into a landscape with the imagery draped over it. Astronauts can rotate an overview, stand at eye level at any stop, or fly the route with a mini-map showing their position. They can pause anywhere and pin a note with a photo, shown as a blue dot that can be edited.
  • A Conditions panel shows daylight and a leave-by time, sky and dust, the radiation dose for the planned walk, temperature and air pressure, each with its NASA source and date. A dust storm, a solar storm or a walk past the 7-hour suit limit turns the plan to No-go.
  • Each stop shows real Perseverance photos taken there and has a sample log with type, notes and photo.
  • A position marker shows where the astronaut is. Mars has no GPS, so on a real mission it would follow the suit’s navigation unit.

Check on the data. NASA’s elevation model matches the heights Perseverance measured at all four stops to within about 3 m.

Benefits and goals. Marswalk gives one screen for one walk: where to go, how steep it is, how long it takes and whether it is safe to go out. We hope it shows how NASA’s open data could support real surface excursions.

Limits. Slope averaged over 20 m misses single boulders. Weather values are the latest NASA publishes, not live readings. The astronaut position, samples and notes are demo data. The slope limits, walking pace and suit limit are our planning assumptions.

Tools. React, Vite, Leaflet, Three.js, JavaScript, Python (NumPy, tifffile, Pillow), hosted on Vercel, with no server or database.
dataRefs: CTX digital terrain model of Jezero, 20 m (USGS Astrogeology, Mars 2020)
Perseverance MEDA weather (temperature, pressure, sunrise, sunset)
Curiosity RAD surface radiation dose: Hassler et al. (2014), “Mars’ Surface Radiation Environment Measured with the Mars Science Laboratory’s Curiosity Rover”, Science 343 (6169),
projectRefs: Spain, Centro de Astrobiología (CAB): the REMS weather station on Curiosity, source of our sky and UV readings.
Inspiration: NASA, “Curiosity’s Proposed Path up Mount Sharp”
Tobler’s hiking function, for walking speed on slopes. Tobler, W. (1993), NCGIA Technical Report 93-1:
A* search algorithm, for route planning. Hart, Nilsson & Raphael (1968)
